title: ASME Audit Support in Cleveland | NDE Joint Review Prep
description: Joint review prep for Northeast Ohio vessel, boiler and forging shops: NDE written practice, Section V procedures, Ohio rules, mock review. Get in touch.
h1: ASME Joint Review Support in Cleveland: NDE Readiness for Northeast Ohio Manufacturers
html:
Northeast Ohio has made boilers, vessels, forgings and valves for well over a century, and many of its shops renew an ASME Certificate of Authorization on a three-year rhythm. If you run quality or NDE at one of them, this page sets out how Atlantis NDT readies the nondestructive examination side of your program for the joint review, and how Ohio's rules affect manufacturers and repair organizations. An Atlantis ASNT NDT Level III does the document work remotely and visits your Cleveland-area plant for the floor checks and the mock review. Start with a short note about your certificate.

Northeast Ohio's pressure equipment makers

The region's industrial base is heavy and old in the best sense. Steel making and forging gave rise to a supply chain of forged and cast pressure parts: nozzles, flanges, tubesheets, valve bodies and fittings. Boiler making and heat recovery equipment have a long history across Northeast Ohio. Fabricators build tanks, reactors and process vessels for the chemical, polymer, coatings and specialty materials plants of the Great Lakes, and for power stations. Many shops are mid-sized, family-owned and decades into their certificates, with a few long-serving people who carry much of the program in their heads.

The state is also where the National Board of Boiler and Pressure Vessel Inspectors is headquartered, in Columbus. That does not give Ohio shops any special treatment, but it does mean the people who write and teach the inspection side of the system are close at hand, and Ohio's own rules lean heavily on the National Board Inspection Code. Our Cleveland NDT consulting page and steel industry NDT consulting page describe the wider local work.

Ohio's rules for boilers and pressure vessels

Ohio's program sits in the Department of Commerce, Division of Industrial Compliance, whose Chief Boiler Inspector leads the state's boiler work; the detailed rules sit in Chapter 4101:4 of the Ohio Administrative Code. Ohio uses its own vocabulary for inspectors: general inspectors work for the state, and special inspectors are employed by insurance companies. Equipment carries an ASME stamp, National Board registration, a state of Ohio boiler number or, for some older units, an "Ohio Special" tag, and the superintendent may issue a certificate of operation after inspection.

The rule on existing boilers and pressure vessels is worth knowing even for a manufacturer, because it shapes the repair work many Ohio shops also do. Routine repairs that involve welding need a permit, and welding must follow Section IX. Major repairs to ASME-stamped or Ohio-numbered equipment follow Part 3 of the NBIC; an organization without an R certificate needs a permit and approval of the repair by a special or general inspector, with a signed repair report to the superintendent. Alterations require an R certificate and approval by an Authorized Inspector. Units that lack an ASME stamp, National Board registration, an Ohio number or an Ohio Special tag generally cannot be reinstalled or relocated in Ohio. Our Ohio NDT consulting and Ohio inspection services pages carry more state context.

Forgings, castings and purchased material

Ohio shops buy and make a lot of forged and cast pressure parts, and that pulls NDE into the material control section of the quality control manual. When a forged tubesheet or nozzle arrives with ultrasonic examination already done by the forge, the certificate holder still has to show that the material specification and any supplementary examination requirements were met, that the material test report and NDE report match the part, and that the part is traceable through fabrication. When the shop does the ultrasonic examination itself, the procedure and the technician must meet Section V and the material specification. Section V Article 23 reproduces SA-388, the standard practice for ultrasonic examination of steel forgings, which is a common reference for this work.

Purchased parts built under someone else's certificate add another layer. Partial data reports, such as the U-2 for Division 1 parts, must arrive with the parts and be reviewed. The joint review team often picks a vessel and works backward through its parts: which supplier, which data report, which NDE, who received it, who checked it. See our Section V Article 23 notes and UT of castings and forgings page for the method side.

Alloy, clad and overlay vessels for the chemical and polymer plants

Process plants around the Great Lakes buy vessels in stainless steel, nickel alloys and clad plate, because the chemistry they run would eat carbon steel. That widens the NDE program in ways a carbon-steel shop never meets. Weld overlay and clad restoration welds are commonly examined by penetrant, which brings contaminant-controlled materials and careful post-cleaning into the procedure. Plate may need ultrasonic examination for laminations or for the bond between cladding and backing steel where the material specification or the purchaser asks for it, and Section V Article 23 also carries the plate standards those orders cite. Some purchasers add ferrite checks, positive material identification or hardness testing. None of those additions are Code examinations, but they sit on the same traveler and are signed by the same people, so the review team will check that they are kept apart from Code NDE and that each is done to a written instruction.

Alloy work also raises a training question. A technician certified for penetrant on carbon steel bench work may never have examined an overlay on a nozzle bore or a clad tubesheet face. Your written practice can require additional training or a practical examination for that kind of work, and a review team that sees the gap between what the certificate covers and what the technician actually does may ask about it. Our training programme setup page explains how to build that into the program rather than leaving it to individual supervisors.

In-house magnetic particle and penetrant work in Ohio shops

Many Northeast Ohio fabricators do their own magnetic particle and penetrant examination with Level II people certified under the company's written practice, and buy radiography from a licensed radiography company. That is a sensible arrangement, and it is where the review team looks for everyday discipline. For magnetic particle work the questions are concrete: Which yokes or prods are in use, and when were their lifting power checks last done? How is field adequacy verified on the part? Are the particles, the bath and any UV-A lamp and meter covered by the procedure and calibrated? For penetrant work: which material batches are in use, what temperature range and dwell does the procedure allow, and does the lighting at the bench meet it?

Each of those answers has to match the procedure the technician was trained on, and the technician has to be current: certification in date, vision examination within its interval, and the experience behind the certification written down. The Section V Article 7 page covers magnetic particle requirements, and our vision examination records page explains how to keep that evidence clean.

Thick sections and ultrasonic procedure qualification

Heavy-wall vessels and forged components push Ohio shops toward ultrasonic examination, sometimes in place of radiography and sometimes alongside it. The review team expects an ultrasonic procedure that names its essential variables, such as the instrument, search units, angles, couplant, scanning technique and calibration reflectors, and, where the Code calls for it, evidence that the procedure was qualified or demonstrated. Calibration blocks have to suit the material and thickness. Where computerized or phased array UT is used, the team will ask how data are stored, reviewed and retained, and who in your organization signs off the evaluation before the Authorized Inspector sees it.

This is often where an older program shows its age: a manual UT procedure written for plate a fraction of the thickness now in production, or a phased array setup run without a procedure that anyone at the shop approved. Our procedure qualification and demonstration service and Section V Article 4 notes explain how to put that right.

R certificate holders and owner maintenance shops

Across Ohio, repair organizations holding the National Board R certificate work on boilers and vessels in mills, chemical plants, hospitals and universities. Examination on a repair is set by the code the item was originally built to, read together with the NBIC, and the NDE reports end up in the repair package the Authorized Inspector checks. Because Ohio's own rules route major repairs and every alteration through NBIC Part 3, the R certificate review and Ohio permits often meet in the same job file. For the National Board side, read our R-stamp NDT audit support notes.

Where Atlantis fits, and where it stops

On the NDE portion of an Ohio joint review, Atlantis does five things. It compares your written practice with whichever SNT-TC-1A or CP-189 edition applies and rewrites it where needed, through our written practice development work. It checks your NDE procedures and technique sheets against Section V and the construction Code and drafts replacements. It audits examiner files and rebuilds missing evidence honestly, as described on our experience log page. It traces purchased-part NDE through your receiving records and drafts the NDE wording your manual needs on material control and subcontracting. And it runs a mock review of the NDE portion with your team, then helps you document corrective action.

The responsibilities that sit elsewhere stay there. The Authorized Inspection Agency accepts your manual and its Inspector signs the data reports; the team recommends and ASME decides; your company certifies its NDE personnel and owns its quality control system. Atlantis performs none of those functions. Welding procedure specifications and the qualification records behind them come from your welding engineer, and Atlantis neither writes nor qualifies them; if you want background, read the WPS, PQR and WPQ explainer. Section III nuclear certificates are outside our scope. Atlantis also takes no radiographs on American soil; reviewing a radiography company's procedures and film as a Level III is the extent of its RT role.

Checklist before a Northeast Ohio review

  1. Confirm the Code edition in your manual, the SNT-TC-1A or CP-189 edition it references, and that your written practice says the same.
  2. Check every in-house MT and PT examiner file for certification dates, vision dates and recorded experience.
  3. Pull yoke lifting power records, UV-A lamp and light meter calibrations, and penetrant batch certifications for the past three years.
  4. Choose two vessels with forged parts and trace each part from purchase order to material test report, NDE report, partial data report if any, and receiving sign-off.
  5. Read your UT procedure against the thickest work you now produce, and confirm calibration blocks match the material.
  6. Assemble the file on your radiography company: written practice, procedures accepted for your work, technician certifications, and your review of the film.
  7. If you do repairs, check that Ohio permits and the R certificate scope line up with recent jobs.
  8. Identify the long-serving people who hold the program in their heads, and make sure what they know is written into the procedures.
  9. Collect corrective-action evidence from the previous review, including proof that each fix was checked on later jobs rather than just written into a revised procedure.
  10. For alloy and clad work, confirm that ferrite, PMI and hardness instructions exist in writing and are recorded separately from Code examinations.
  11. List every technician who examined overlays or clad surfaces since the last review and check that their training covered that kind of work.
  12. Run a practice interview with each person who holds a quality duty.

What to send and how we work

Send the designators and scope on your certificate, your expected review month, the manual sections covering examination, NDE, material control, subcontracting and records, your written practice and your procedure list. We work through them remotely and return a gap list tied to the manual and the Code, then come to your plant to sample records, check equipment and run the mock review. We reply within one business day. For technicians who need formal training, our NDT training for Cleveland follows SNT-TC-1A, with certification remaining your company's decision under its written practice. Our ASME audit Level III support overview lists everything in the service, and nearby manufacturers in Western Pennsylvania can read our Pittsburgh ASME audit support page.

faq.q: What does Ohio mean by a general inspector and a special inspector?
faq.a: A general inspector works for the state; a special inspector is employed by an insurance company. Ohio's rules let either approve many repairs and inspect equipment before operation, while alterations and repairs under an R certificate are approved by an Authorized Inspector.

faq.q: Do welded repairs in Ohio need a permit?
faq.a: Under Ohio's rule on existing boilers and pressure vessels, routine repairs that involve welding require a permit, and major repairs to stamped or Ohio-numbered equipment follow NBIC Part 3. Check the current rule and your AIA for a specific job.

faq.q: Our forgings arrive with UT already done by the forge. What will the team want to see?
faq.a: That the material specification and any supplementary examination were met, that the material test report and NDE report match the part, that the part is traceable, and that someone in your organization reviewed the documents on receipt.

faq.q: Who approves our ultrasonic procedure for heavy-wall work?
faq.a: Your written practice assigns it, normally to a Level III. Where the Code requires qualification or demonstration of the procedure, keep the record. Our procedure development page explains the process.

faq.q: Our long-time Level III has retired. What should we do before the review?
faq.a: Name a new Level III in the written practice, have that person review and re-approve the procedures, and check that examinations given since the retirement were given by someone qualified. An outside Level III can fill the role; see Level III consulting.

faq.q: Can Atlantis prepare certification records for our MT and PT examiners?
faq.a: We can audit them, show where evidence is missing and help you rebuild it from real records. We will not create records for training or experience that did not happen.

faq.q: Does it matter that the National Board is headquartered in Ohio?
faq.a: Not for how your review is run. It is simply where the National Board is based, and Ohio's rules refer to the NBIC throughout.
Our Cleveland NDT training and Level 2 courses follow SNT-TC-1A. Completing a course does not certify anyone; your company does that under its written practice.

faq.q: Is nuclear Section III work part of this service?
faq.a: No. Section III nuclear certificates are outside our scope.
